article_title: Practice-Driven Data
citation: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: To&Through Online Tool: a public-facing data tool disaggregating Chicago high school outcomes by prior achievement
description: The To&Through Online Tool is a public-facing data tool with data on all Chicago public high schools, developed by the To&Through Project using Consortium research on middle-grade indicators. It disaggregates freshman course performance by eighth-grade GPA and attendance — combined into summary measures estimating a student's risk and opportunity for success or struggle in ninth grade — and shows how comparison schools with similar incoming students are faring. Its displays are designed for simplicity and practice use: one graph begins with a question framing the data's purpose, uses a simple stacked line graph, allows disaggregation by student group such as moderately qualified graduates, and integrates high school and college data from different sources to prompt questions about how shifts in practice led to changes in outcomes.
requirements: Underlying Consortium research identifying eighth-grade GPA and attendance as the most powerful predictors of ninth-grade performance
Integration of high school and college data from different sources into one interface
constraints: The paper presents the tool in the Chicago context, where over 90 district-run high schools serve dramatically different populations
target_learners: high school educators and school leaders
target_learning_goals: tracking freshman on-track and college enrollment outcomes
placing school results in context against comparison schools
examples: Figure 6 shows a To&Through graph of college enrollment rates for moderately qualified graduates over time at a sample school, splitting enrollment between 2-year and 4-year colleges
key_sources: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/practice-driven-data-lessons-chicagos-approach-research-data-and-practice-education

constraints: The pathway work is specific to two Kentucky districts, Pikeville Independent and Floyd County Schools

article_title: Inclusive Innovation: Increasing Recruitment and Retention of Teachers of Color
citation: Inclusive Innovation: Increasing Recruitment and Retention of Teachers of Color — Summation of Digital Promise Design Studios with Teachers of Color. (2021). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org/inclusive-innovation/
title: Three-phase Design Studio structure: need statements, solution ideas, solution concepts
description: The Design Studio process is a three-phase co-design pattern grounded in the Inclusive Innovation model. Phase I uses need statement 'madlibs' where teachers take personas to identify key issues; Phase II has participants 'stretch' their ideas to be bold and innovative in breakout groups; Phase III has Advisory Council teachers create solution concepts describing value proposition, success statement, outcomes, and benefits. Each studio ran over two days.
requirements: Teachers of color lead the process rather than serving as consulted participants
Structured persona-taking during need identification

target_learning_goals: identifying root causes of recruitment and retention challenges
generating actionable solution concepts
examples: 88 teachers of color across six Design Studios produced need statements, solution ideas, and fourteen solution concepts presented at a national showcase

article_title: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection
citation: Aimee Evan, Hannah Sullivan, and Laura Groth (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://ncsrc.info
title: Tool #1: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Your Portfolio worksheet
description: Tool #1 is a reflective worksheet for authorizers. Its stated purpose is to "determine how indicators may appear in data and in practice, reflect on these data, and identify indicators of distress in their own portfolio." Users review seven indicator tables, check which indicators struggling portfolio schools exhibited, add context-specific examples, and reflect on which indicators are most relevant and why schools in their context may be experiencing them. Estimated time is 1.5 hours.
requirements: Data collection reports, such as site visits, annual reports, and renewal reports from schools in the portfolio
constraints: Recommended for team use with members monitoring academic, financial, and operational performance
target_learners: Charter school authorizers and other stakeholders supporting charter schools
target_learning_goals: Recognizing distress indicators in their own portfolio of schools
examples: Users check boxes next to evidence such as high or increased leader turnover or decreased student enrollment
key_sources: Aimee Evan, Hannah Sullivan, and Laura Groth (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED616212

article_title: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection
citation: Aimee Evan, Hannah Sullivan, and Laura Groth (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://ncsrc.info
title: Tool #2: Auditing Your Data Collection for Indicators of Distress
description: Tool #2 supports authorizers in "reviewing their data collection methods to determine where they are already collecting data on indicators and to close gaps to improve the identification of schools in distress." It maps each distress indicator to example artifacts and sources—board minutes, check-ins, audits, enrollment data, staff retention data—and asks authorizers to document informal versus formal collection mechanisms and identify gaps. Estimated time is 30 minutes.
requirements: Data collection instruments, such as site visit protocols, annual reports, performance management frameworks
constraints: The report advises that revamping data collection is not likely needed; minor modifications to existing methods suffice
target_learning_goals: Auditing and improving data collection to identify schools in distress
examples: The report suggests adding teacher attendance data to annual reporting and including a professional-culture question in site visit protocols

article_title: The Search for More Complex Racial and Ethnic Representation in Grade School Books
citation: Tanji Reed Marshall, Ph.D., and William H. Rodick, Ph.D. (2023). The Search for More: Complex Racial and Ethnic Representation in Grade School Books. The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/booktool
title: Tool for Representational Balance in Books
description: A 10-criterion rubric, developed by The Education Trust after convening experts, consulting publishers, and synthesizing existing cultural-responsiveness and bias tools, designed to "guide a reader through any text to determine how people, cultures, and topics are represented." Its four sections cover creator and character identity, people, cultures, and topics, with each criterion framed as a question (e.g., "Are people of color multidimensional?"). The team applied it to 300 K-8 trade books from EdReports-favorably rated curricula, coding representations as complex, partial, or limited, and offers it publicly at edtrust.org/booktool for publishers, district leaders, educators, caregivers, and students.
requirements: Applied to texts by readers analyzing how people, cultures, and topics are represented; in this study it was applied to core trade books identified by publishers as expected reading for all students
constraints: The report acknowledges its ethnoracial grouping methods are imperfect and obscure distinctions across and within groups; identities present in the sampled books were not complex, limiting intersectional analysis
target_learners: K-8 students reading ELA curricula texts
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking about how people, cultures, and historical and social topics are represented in texts
examples: Applied to 300 K-8 books selected from trade book lists of publisher partners whose curricula partially or fully met EdReports quality measures, reaching at least 25% saturation per publisher and per grade band (K-2, 3-5, 6-8)

article_title: From digital transformation to intelligent classrooms: artificial intelligence, adaptive leadership, and service delivery in global higher education—a systematic literature review
citation: Nyamboga TO (2026) From digital transformation to intelligent classrooms: artificial intelligence, adaptive leadership, and service delivery in global higher education—a systematic literature review. Front. Educ. 11:1899369. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1899369
title: Integrated TOE, socio-technical systems, and adaptive leadership framework for AI-enabled intelligent classrooms and service delivery transformation
description: The review grounds its synthesis in an integrated conceptual framework combining the Technology–Organisation–Environment (TOE) framework, Socio-Technical Systems (STS) theory, and Adaptive Leadership theory. Within it, AI is "the central technological driver enabling the development of intelligent learning environments and automated institutional systems," adaptive leadership is "the organisational mechanism that supports change management, institutional alignment, and stakeholder engagement," and service delivery outcomes are the performance dimension reflecting efficiency, responsiveness, accessibility, and student satisfaction. TOE explains institutional adoption patterns; STS explains alignment between technical infrastructure and social structures; adaptive leadership explains how leaders mobilise institutions to address complex technological challenges.
requirements: Institutional readiness, leadership capacity, digital infrastructure, financial resources, staff competencies, and organisational culture as conditions the framework identifies for AI-driven transformation
constraints: The framework is developed for higher education institutions and its components are shaped by internal organisational conditions and external environmental pressures
Leadership-related findings carry moderate certainty due to contextual variability across regions
target_learning_goals: institutional digital transformation
AI-enabled service delivery improvement
adaptive leadership capacity for technological change
examples: The review used the framework to structure its thematic synthesis of 155 studies across five domains: AI integration, adaptive leadership, infrastructure readiness, service delivery transformation, and barriers to sustainability

description: The article proposes an empirically validated model integrating the Technology–Organisation–Environment (TOE) framework with Diffusion of Innovations (DOI) theory to explain AI adoption in universities. Structural equation modelling to test hypothesised relationships

article_title: Peer Assessment Between Students in Colleges and Universities
citation: Keith Topping. (1998). Peer Assessment Between Students in Colleges and Universities. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543068003249
title: Topping's definition and 17-parameter typology of peer assessment in higher education
description: The article defines peer assessment as "an arrangement in which individuals consider the amount, level, value, worth, quality, or success of the products or outcomes of learning of peers of similar status", restricted to students of similar degree status in higher education. It then develops a typology of 17 parameters of variation (Table 1), including curriculum area, objectives, formative/summative focus, product, relation to staff assessment, directionality, privacy, contact, year, ability, constellations, place, time, requirement and reward. The typology was developed "from immersion in this literature" and warns that sweeping general conclusions are unlikely to be meaningful.
requirements: Projects must be situated on the typology's parameters, since activities vary widely and general conclusions require specifying the configuration
constraints: Excludes paid postgraduates grading undergraduates as surrogate staff members; concerns peers of similar status in higher education
target_learning_goals: formative and summative assessment of peer products and outcomes
examples: The Falchikov (1995a) case study is characterized as a same-year, bilaterally quantitative and qualitative, in-class, compulsory, supplementary, mutual group peer assessment system in oral presentation skills

article_title: Intelligence, creativity, and cognitive control: The common and differential involvement of executive functions in intelligence and creativity
citation: Benedek Mathias, Jauk Emanuel, Sommer Markus, Arendasy Martin, Neubauer Aljoscha C. (2014). Intelligence, creativity, and cognitive control: The common and differential involvement of executive functions in intelligence and creativity. Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.intell.2014.05.007
title: Assess creativity via rated quality of top ideas rather than ideational fluency to avoid confounding with response count
description: The article scored divergent thinking tasks by the top-scoring method, in which creativity scores reflect the average creativity rating of the three highest-rated ideas per task. The authors state this method "was shown to avoid a confounding with the number of responses", allowing latent creativity to reflect the creative quality of ideas rather than sheer output volume. Four raters scored responses holistically on a four-point scale considering originality and appropriateness.
requirements: Multiple experienced raters with acceptable interrater reliability (ICC values reported between .57 and .79)
constraints: Requires holistic rating judgments; the article notes high creativity ratings should only be assigned to ideas that only few people could presumably come up with
target_learning_goals: assessment of creative potential (divergent thinking ability)
examples: Four DT tasks (two alternate uses, two instances) were administered with 2 min per task, and creativity scores reflected the average rating of the three top-rated ideas per task

article_title: Top-down modulation: bridging selective attention and working memory
citation: Gazzaley A, Nobre AC. (2012). Top-down modulation: Bridging selective attention and working memory. Trends in Cognitive Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tics.2011.11.014
title: Top-down modulation as a common neural mechanism bridging selective attention and working memory
description: The review proposes that top-down modulation — modulation of neural activity in lower-order sensory areas based on an individual's goals — serves as a common framework for selective attention and working memory. Its core features are "activity modulation in stimulus-selective sensory cortices with concurrent engagement of prefrontal and parietal control regions that function as sources of top-down signals". The mechanism operates across all working memory stages, both when stimuli are present and absent.
requirements: Evidence from human neurophysiological methods (fMRI, EEG/ERP, TMS) indexing sensory-cortex modulation and prefrontal-parietal control engagement
constraints: The review focuses on human neurophysiological studies of visual working memory and delayed-response paradigms
target_learning_goals: understanding the neural mechanisms supporting attention and working memory

article_title: Contributions of executive function and spatial skills to preschool mathematics achievement
citation: Verdine, B. N., Irwin, C. M., Golinkoff, R. M., & Hirsh-Pasek, K. (2014). Contributions of Executive Function and Spatial Skills to Preschool Mathematics Achievement. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 126, 37-51. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2014.02.012
title: Test of Spatial Assembly (TOSA): a 2-D and 3-D spatial assembly assessment designed for 3-year-olds
description: The TOSA is a non-verbal spatial assembly task created specifically as an assessment for 3-year-olds, comprising 2-D trials recreating pictured designs with magnetized foam shapes and 3-D trials recreating glued Mega Blocks models. It was built because few appropriate spatial tasks exist for 3-year-olds; the article reports "Cronbach's alpha was .802 for all trials that made up the TOSA." Scores are z-scored per portion and averaged.
requirements: Administered individually with trained coders scoring photographs of constructions, with inter-rater agreement of 96-97% as reported
constraints: Designed for and validated with 3-year-old children; the article notes most spatial assessments start at age 4
target_learning_goals: Early geometric and spatial reasoning, including part/whole composition and object relative position
examples: 2-D trials used six target designs on magnetic whiteboards with two to four foam shape pieces; 3-D trials used six Mega Blocks models, with items 1 and 2 at ceiling and excluded from scoring

article_title: Appropriation of a shared workspace: Organizing principles and their application
citation: Overdijk, M. & van Diggelen, W. (2008). Appropriation of a shared workspace: Organizing principles and their application. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-008-9038-4
title: Tool appropriation as mutual shaping between learners and technology
description: The paper defines tool appropriation as a process in which learners make sense of a tool's properties and find 'a way of doing' to carry out their task, constructing essential characteristics of the tool while working with it. Mutual shaping is central: "the actions of the learner are shaped through interaction with the tool, while at the same time the effects of the tool are shaped through the learner's actions." Appropriation becomes manifest during critical events, such as when learners lack directions for use or a use has an unexpected effect.
requirements: Groups must coordinate their exploratory effort and arrive at shared conventions of use
constraints: The concept is developed for small-group appropriation of collaborative technology in classroom settings over relatively short periods
target_learners: secondary school students collaborating with CSCL tools
target_learning_goals: collaborative argumentation and discussion
examples: The study examined how seven groups of three students appropriated a graphical shared workspace during a two-lesson role-play discussion about the public image of Spanish Salou

article_title: Highlighting tools and technologies for collaborative learning
citation: Carolyn P. Rosé, Nancy Law, Ulrike Cress, Sten Ludvigsen. (2019). Highlighting tools and technologies for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. (2019) 14:1–6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09297-z
title: Position tool and technology contributions as first-class citizens alongside theory contributions in CSCL
description: The editorial argues that development of methods, tools, and technologies for CSCL, though often positioned in a less privileged place behind theory about human cognition and social processes, deserves affirmation as first-class contributions. It highlights that CSCL work regularly relegates tools to the background, and presents this special issue to affirm "the society's and the journal's valuing of the tools and technologies that serve to enable this important work."
requirements: Tools work best when the agency they afford is foregrounded in analysis rather than relegated to the background

citation: Daniel Cebrián-Robles; Antonio-Joaquín Franco-Mariscal; Ángel Blanco-López. (2018). Preservice Elementary Science Teachers' Argumentation Competence: Impact of a Training Programme. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9446-4
title: Toulmin's simplified argument model (evidence, justification, conclusion) as the basis for training and assessing argumentation competence
description: The article operationalises argumentation competence through a simplification of Toulmin's model suggested by Jiménez-Aleixandre (2010), reduced to three essential elements that a good argument must have: evidence (facts in Toulmin's model), justification (warrant) and conclusion (claim). PESTs must first identify these three elements in an argument and use them to design rubrics to assess arguments; only once this objective is achieved may the model consider further elements such as previous or backing ideas, and rebuttals or refutations. The three-element version was used to build the study's basic and specific assessment rubrics and its 0–100 overall argumentative quality score.

constraints: The simplified three-element version omits backing ideas and rebuttals/refutations, which are introduced only as a later extension

Critical thinking about science

description: The Topic Checklist is an instrument developed at the University of Limburg to measure what students actually study during self-directed learning. It "consists of a list of topics specifying the intended course content". Students rate on a five-point Likert scale how much time they spent studying each topic and their degree of mastery, allowing researchers to compare actual self-study with student-generated learning issues.

article_title: How to improve argumentation comprehension in university students: experimental test of a training approach
citation: Sarah von der Mühlen, Tobias Richter, Sebastian Schmid, Kirsten Berthold. (2019). How to improve argumentation comprehension in university students: experimental test of a training approach. Instructional Science 47:215–237. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9471-3
title: Toulmin model of argument structure
description: The article adopts Toulmin's (1958) model as the theoretical basis for its training, in which full-fledged informal arguments are deconstructed into functional components. According to the article, "full-fledged arguments contain a number of functional key components: a claim, reason(s) (or datum/data), a warrant, backing evidence, and a rebuttal". The warrant is treated as central for scientific literacy because it determines whether a conclusion is justified given the data, and warrants and backing are often implicit and hardest to identify.
requirements: Learners must be able to distinguish claim, datum, warrant, backing, and rebuttal within authentic argumentative texts
constraints: Warrants and backing evidence are often not explicitly stated in everyday arguments and must be inferred by the reader

scientific literacy
examples: The article illustrates the model with an argument about eggs and cholesterol, labelling claim, datum, warrant, backing, and rebuttal sentences

article_title: The many facets of metacognition: comparing multiple measures of metacognition in healthy individuals
citation: Terneusen, A., Quaedflieg, C., van Heugten, C., Ponds, R., & Winkens, I. (2024). The many facets of metacognition: comparing multiple measures of metacognition in healthy individuals. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09350-1
title: Neuropsychological model of metacognition: metacognitive knowledge and online awareness (monitoring and self-regulation)
description: The article adopts a neuropsychological model in which "Two main elements of metacognition... are metacognitive knowledge and online awareness". Metacognitive knowledge is stable knowledge and beliefs about one's cognitive processes and strategies stored in long-term memory; online awareness is flexible, task-context-dependent evaluation of performance, comprising monitoring (anticipating performance and error recognition) and self-regulation (changing strategies in response to task demands). The study uses this structure to organize its measures and test which elements predict metacognitive sensitivity.
requirements: Measures must be matched to the element being assessed: questionnaires for metacognitive knowledge, performance-based confidence and discrepancy measures for online awareness
constraints: The article notes online awareness depends on task characteristics such as complexity and familiarity, and personal factors such as motivation and meaningfulness of the task
target_learners: populations with metacognitive impairments such as after brain disorders (proposed application)
target_learning_goals: accurate self-monitoring of performance
self-regulation of strategies during learning tasks
examples: The study operationalized the model's elements as MAI subscales, prospective and retrospective discrepancy scores, and trial-by-trial confidence ratings yielding AUROC2

article_title: The process of early self-control: an observational study in two- and three-year-olds
citation: Mulder, H., van Ravenswaaij, H., Verhagen, J., Moerbeek, M., & Leseman, P. P. M. (2019). The process of early self-control: an observational study in two- and three-year-olds. Metacognition and Learning, 14, 239–264. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-019-09199-3
title: Active hand withholding in toddlers as a rudimentary form of situation modification
description: The article interprets toddlers' active hand-withholding behaviours — holding hands under the table, crossing the arms, or holding one hand tightly with the other — as blocking the direct route to the reward, and relates this to the adult and older-child literature: "this may be seen as a form of 'situation modification'". It situates the behaviour within theoretical accounts (the hot/cool systems framework and the process model of self-control) in which self-control is facilitated by shifting attention away from the reward or making reaching more effortful. The authors note Gross's original definition of situation modification does not seem to fully cover these behaviours, since the toddlers act without changing the situation itself.
requirements: A delay-of-gratification setting in which the reward is physically present and within reach, so that blocking the direct reaching route is possible
constraints: The article notes Gross's (2015) definition of situation modification as directly altering a situation does not fully seem to cover these toddler behaviours, so the mapping is interpretive rather than exact
target_learning_goals: exerting self-control and delaying gratification in the presence of an immediate reward
examples: Children were observed to hold their hands under the table, cross their arms, or hold one hand tightly with the other during 60-s snack and gift delay tasks

article_title: Improving norms in research culture to incentivize transparency and rigor
citation: Mellor, D. (2021). Improving norms in research culture to incentivize transparency and rigor. Educational Psychologist, 56(2). https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3125-5888
title: TOP Guidelines for transparency and openness in publishing and funding
description: The Transparency and Openness Promotion (TOP) Guidelines, developed in 2014 among social scientists, editors, and funders, are a policy framework for journals and funders. The article states they "cover eight specific standards where open science can be practiced in publishing and funding", including data citation; data, materials, and code transparency; design and analysis transparency; preregistration; and replication research. Each standard has three levels of increasing rigor, and TOP provides specific policy recommendations and a plan for increasing rigor over time.
requirements: Journals and funders select which of the eight standards and levels to adopt; Level 2 mandates transparency with exceptions only for legal or ethical constraints, and Level 3 requires verification or computational reproducibility
constraints: Level 0 represents the ineffective status quo and is not compliant with TOP; the article notes data sharing in education research raises ethical and legal feasibility limits that policies must accommodate
target_learning_goals: adopting journal and funder policies that incentivize transparency, preregistration, and reproducibility
examples: The article describes a signatory campaign with over 5,000 journals, societies, publishers, and funders, and the TOP Factor rubric that awards 0 to 3 points per standard

citation: Lewis M. Terman and Clara Harbison Town. (1917). Communications and Discussions, The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org

citation: Patricia A Alexander. (2016). Relational thinking and relational reasoning: harnessing the power of patterning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.4
title: TORR family of relational reasoning measures (TORR, vTORR, TORRjr)
description: The article describes three psychometric measures of relational reasoning developed to move beyond the field's overreliance on the Raven's Matrices and figural analogical items. The TORR is figural and intended as a more fluid measure; the vTORR uses linguistic content and was conceived as somewhat more crystallized, though its novel items still entail flexible problem solving; and the TORRjr is an easier version for children and early adolescents paralleling the TORR in scales, items, and format. The measures can be "easily administered to children, adolescence, and adults either online or in print".

article_title: Reading experience reveals shared and idiosyncratic neural patterns during text comprehension
citation: Song, M., Li, L., He, D. & Cai, Q. (2025). Reading experience reveals shared and idiosyncratic neural patterns during text comprehension. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00390-7
title: Topicalized Author Recognition Test (tART)
description: The tART is a new instrument the authors developed to measure reading experience as a distribution across topics rather than only an overall quantity of print exposure. It included "135 author names spanning 9 topics/genres", with "Each topic comprised 10 real author names and 5 foils", and five response options scored 0 to 4 covering recognition and books read. Topic distributions were converted with a SoftMax transform into probability distributions, whose pairwise KL divergence quantified dissimilarity in reading experience among participants. In this study the maximum exposure score was 360, the sample's mean was 45.844 (SD = 24.975), and scores were validated against self-reported reading frequency (Spearman r = 0.744).
requirements: Topics must have at least 10 authors specialized in the domain who have each published at least three books, to allow reliable topic profiling
A pilot phase to select author names spanning a wide range of recognition difficulty, and a false-alarm-rate scaling factor to correct overclaiming
constraints: The tART covered only nine topics within the participants' native language, omitting science, technology and some social-science categories, biasing it toward literary and humanities-related author knowledge
ART-based measures cannot fully account for individual variability in attention to or memory for author names
It assesses the quantitative amount of exposure rather than qualitative dimensions such as depth of engagement
target_learners: Adult native-language readers (college students aged 18–24 in this study)
target_learning_goals: Profiling reading experience across topics and genres for research on language and reading processing
examples: Author names were drawn from categories on popular Chinese online book stores and reading apps (Jingdong Books, Dangdang, Weixin), with foreign translated authors excluded to limit assessment to the native language

article_title: ToTCompute: A Novel EEG-Based TimeOnTask Threshold Computation Mechanism for Engagement Modelling and Monitoring
citation: Ghergulescu, I. & Muntean, C. H. (2016). ToTCompute: A Novel EEG-Based TimeOnTask Threshold Computation Mechanism for Engagement Modelling and Monitoring. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0111-2
title: ToTCompute mechanism for automatic computation of task-dependent TimeOnTask engagement thresholds
description: ToTCompute is a mechanism that automatically computes TimeOnTask threshold values for various game tasks using game-playing logs and EEG engagement data collected during an initial testing session. It computes "the relative engagement changes for all participants every second (i.e., every TimeOnTask iteration)" and applies a time series linear model with an autocorrelation test, returning NA when data is random or the trend is not negative. Thresholds represent upper limits above which engagement decreases by a predefined relative change (e.g., 5, 10, 15%).
requirements: An initial testing session with at least 30 participants playing while wearing the Emotiv EPOC headset
The game creator must identify independent game tasks within the game
constraints: The algorithm returns NA when the autocorrelation test indicates random data or when the time series linear model is not statistically significant or lacks a negative trend
target_learning_goals: engagement monitoring and modelling during game-based learning

The authors observe that "new tools open up new ways of learner-textbook interaction, which generates new types of data that can, in turn, power the development of new tools." They note this cycle existed before in intelligent educational systems but has accelerated and become more evident with new AI technologies, and that chatbots need calibration based on real teacher-learner interaction data.

constraints: LLM context length is limited and not enough to cover long documents

citation: Huang, S. C.-F., Chen, Z.-H., Lin, Y.-T., & Yeh, M. K. (2026). Bridging strategy gaps in programming: the role of visual scaffolding for learners with low cognitive ability. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10684-1

article_title: Capturing Students' Attention: An Empirical Study
citation: Rosegard, E., & Wilson, J. (2013). Capturing students' attention: An empirical study. Journal of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, Vol. 13, No. 5, December 2013. https://josotl.indiana.edu
title: Open a lecture with a brief, topic-relevant, novel external stimulus (attention grabber) to elevate arousal and improve information retention
description: This principle recommends beginning a class with a short external stimulus — a hook, trigger, attention getter/grabber, or anticipatory set — that is novel and germane to the course content, based on the framework that "an external stimulus will evoke arousal, focus attention, and result in information retention." The article's experiment supported a significant but small retention benefit from a 90-second topic-relevant stimulus. It cautions that the stimulus should contain collative properties (novelty, ambiguity, surprise) and produce moderate arousal, since too much arousal leads to anxiety and too little to boredom.
requirements: The external stimulus must be topic-relevant/germane to the course content
It should contain collative properties such as novelty, ambiguity, or surprise
It should produce a moderate level of arousal
constraints: The measured benefit was small (Cohen's d = 0.35; less than a 1-point advantage on a 15-point exam), and the article questions whether the incremental change is worth the time and effort
No research was found identifying an optimal level of arousal, optimal stimulus duration, or timing (pre- vs. post-learning) for external stimuli in classroom settings
Generalizability is limited due to a dearth of empirical evidence examining external stimuli and information retention in classroom settings
target_learners: college students in general education courses
target_learning_goals: retention of lecture information
examples: In the four-year experiment, the arousal condition used a 90-second alcohol-related poem (years one and four), a 90-second paired movement game called "no need for alcohol" (year two), and a 90-second word search puzzle in a 15x15 letter grid (year three), each followed by the same 30-minute lecture and 15-point exam

title: Total Physical Response (TPR) method
description: TPR is a language teaching method developed by James Asher in 1965 that teaches language through the coordination of speech and physical action. The article defines it as "a language teaching method that attempts to teach language through physical (motor) activity", associated with tracking theory involving intense repetition of verbal and physical activity. Its principles include teaching grammar inductively, delaying speech until comprehension forms, learning in a low-stress environment, and the teacher centrally selecting commands; meanings are indicated by actions rather than explained one by one, beginning with imperative moods and realia.
requirements: The teacher must master the spoken language, develop understanding with body language, and get students ready to speak
Students should not be corrected directly and are not forced to speak; exposure, understanding, and physical reactions precede speech
constraints: It is more effective with beginners and young students, especially ages 7-11
Stated disadvantages include that it is limited since everything cannot be explained by this method, is easy to overuse, and should be combined with other approaches
target_learners: young and beginner foreign language learners (preschool, primary, secondary) and adult university learners
target_learning_goals: foreign/second language vocabulary learning and lexical competence
examples: The 13 meta-analysis studies implemented TPR across preschool to university levels, several supporting it with songs, stories, games, pictures/flashcards and realia, and pair work activities.

title: Top-down model of personality, self-regulation, coping and achievement emotions
description: The article interprets its results within a top-down model in which the relatively stable personality construct materializes in behavior through self-regulation, which in turn relates to coping strategies and achievement emotions. The authors state self-regulation "may be considered a behavioral materialization of personality factors" and argue the same holds for coping strategies and achievement emotions, with a similar pattern across class, study and testing situations. The three SEM models in Table 4 instantiate this linear associative chain.
requirements: Measures of personality (Big Five), self-regulation, coping strategies and achievement emotions in the same sample to estimate the linear relations
constraints: The article states the design is correlational, so the observed relationships may reflect other confounding variables and experimental and longitudinal evidence is needed for mechanistic and directional claims
target_learning_goals: emotional health and achievement-emotion regulation in academic contexts
examples: Three SEMs (class, study, test situations) with personality positively predicting self-regulation, self-regulation negatively predicting coping and negative emotions, and emotion-focused coping positively predicting negative emotions

title: Tobin's 3-dimensional framework (emancipatory, coparticipatory, qualia) used to evaluate the blended learning environment
description: The article applies Tobin's 3-dimensional framework for evaluating participants' perception of the web-based environment to interpret the CTBL program's effects. The authors write: "On the basis of Tobin's [61] 3-dimensional framework to evaluate participants' perception of the web-based environment, we evaluated the CTBL program." The emancipatory dimension (the WCP) let participants control pace, place, and depth of learning; the coparticipatory dimension (case-based approach) provided a platform to explore and discuss clinical teaching options with peers and instructors; and the qualia dimension captured participants' enjoyment of the program.
requirements: Used to interpret perceptions of a web-based/blended learning environment, requiring both web-based and face-to-face components to evaluate all three dimensions
constraints: The article uses the framework interpretively to structure its discussion; it does not test the framework itself
target_learners: Registered nurse preceptors in continuing professional education
target_learning_goals: Clinical teaching competency
Positive attitudes toward web-based learning
examples: The authors map the WCP to the emancipatory dimension, the case-based approach to the coparticipatory dimension, and overall enjoyment to the qualia dimension

title: TOSLS: a freely available 28-item multiple-choice test of scientific literacy skills for Gen Ed biology courses
description: The Test of Scientific Literacy Skills is a multiple-choice assessment contextualized around real-world problems, designed to be quick to administer and score in large-enrollment courses. The article states that "The instrument consists of 28 multiple-choice questions that are contextualized around real-world problems," such as evaluating the reliability of an Internet site or determining what evidence would support a fitness product's effectiveness. It was developed through five semester-long pilot-and-revision cycles and is freely available with its answer key in the Supplemental Material.
requirements: Administered the same way when used for cross-course or cross-institution comparisons, per the article: comparisons are reliable only when the assessment is administered the same way
constraints: Developed using items administered to Gen Ed students in biology courses at a large research university; validity for science disciplines beyond biology needs more research, per the authors
target_learners: Undergraduate nonmajors and majors in introductory/general education biology courses
target_learning_goals: Scientific literacy skills: evaluating scientific arguments, sources, research design, and quantitative data
examples: Administered pre- and postsemester in five courses at three institution types, including a project-based nonmajors course and a traditional lecture-based nonmajors course

title: Two-category, nine-skill taxonomy of measurable scientific literacy skills
description: The TOSLS articulates scientific literacy as nine measurable skills in two categories: skills related to "recognizing and analyzing the use of methods of inquiry that lead to scientific knowledge" (identifying valid scientific arguments, evaluating source validity, evaluating use and misuse of scientific information, understanding research design) and skills related to organizing, analyzing, and interpreting quantitative data and scientific information (creating and reading graphs, quantitative problem solving, interpreting statistics, justifying inferences). requirements: Skills must be articulated as measurable outcomes to evaluate student mastery, as the authors did in Table 2
constraints: Grounded in NRC and Project 2061 definitions of scientific literacy as the framework for the working concept
target_learning_goals: Scientific literacy: methods of inquiry and quantitative data interpretation
examples: Faculty survey responses were classified against the nine skills; the most frequent responses aligned with understanding the nature of science

description: Élément matériel permettant de réaliser et enregistrer des figures de speckle à faible coût sur un banc d'optique : laser He-Ne, verre dépoli, diaphragme calibré et webcam dont l'objectif est retiré. L'article précise : "nous avons utilisé une webcam Toucam Pro 2  munie du capteur Sony ICX098BQ. Ce capteur est constitué de 659 x 494 pixels" avec "le pas de notre capteur est de 5,6 µm". constraints: Les enregistrements se font directement sur la CCD, objectif dévissé, pour éviter le champ de speckles subjectifs causé par l'optique de la webcam ; pour les interférences, L > 1 m pour se placer en conditions de Fraunhofer.
target_learners: étudiants en optique de niveau universitaire (enseignement de la physique)
target_learning_goals: comprendre le phénomène de speckle
maîtriser l'optique de Fourier (produit, convolution)
ancrer les interférences à 2 et N ondes et la diffraction par les réseaux

TF de superpositions de 2 à 20 figures de speckle décalées (Figures 8 à 15)
Mesure de la séparation de Gamma Leo au télescope Meade ETX 125
